prompt_sources.problem:

I. ${D}_{1}(y)=xy\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$

II. ${D}_{2}(y)={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$

III. ${D}_{3}(y)={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-y$

prompt_sources.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

I. ${D}_{1}(y)={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}y$

II. ${D}_{2}(y)=y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y$

III. ${D}_{3}(y)=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy$

III only

solution_sources.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+{x}^{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{x}^{2}{y}_{1}+a{x}^{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =a[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}{y}_{1}]+b[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{x}^{2}{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2})\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is **not** linear.
To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+2(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})+2a{y}_{1}+2b{y}_{2} \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})+2a{y}_{1}+2b{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2}) & =a[{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+2{y}_{1}]+b[{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+2{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+2a{y}_{1}+2b{y}_{2}.\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+x(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ax{y}_{1}+bx{y}_{2} \\  & =a[\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+x{y}_{1}]+b[\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+x{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2})\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator $L,$ we have the linearity condition

$$
L(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aL({y}_{1})+bL({y}_{2})
$$

for functions ${y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x),$ and where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

For the given differential operator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+{(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}))}^{2} \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{(a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2} \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+2ab\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2} \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+{b}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2} \\  & +2ab\cdot (\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}).\end{aligned}
$$

This is *not* the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}) & =a[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}]+b[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}] \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+b{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\ne aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}),$ the operator $D$ is $\text{nonlinear}.$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator $L,$ we have the linearity condition

$$
L(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aL({y}_{1})+bL({y}_{2})
$$

for functions ${y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x),$ and where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

For the given differential operator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}))}^{2}+(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & ={(a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2} \\  & ={a}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+2ab\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2} \\  & +a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2} \\  & ={a}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+{b}^{2}{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2} \\  & +ab\cdot (2\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}).\end{aligned}
$$

This is *not* the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}) & =a[{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+{y}_{1}]+b[{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+b{(\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})}^{2}+a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\ne aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}),$ the operator $D$ is $\text{nonlinear}.$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator $L,$ we have the linearity condition

$$
L(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aL({y}_{1})+bL({y}_{2})
$$

for functions ${y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x),$ and where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

For the given differential operator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})-2(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x})-2(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+ab{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ab{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}-2a{y}_{1}-2b{y}_{2} \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}-2\cdot (a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & +ab\cdot ({y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}) \\ .\end{aligned}
$$

This is *not* the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}) & =a[{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}-2{y}_{1}]+b[{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}-2{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}-2(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\ne aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}),$ the operator $D$ is $\text{nonlinear}.$

I. ${D}_{1}(y)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$

II. ${D}_{2}(y)=2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$

III. ${D}_{3}(y)={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$

choices.html: III only
I only

solution_sources.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is **not** linear. To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2}) & =a[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}.\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})-x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =2a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-ax\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}-bx\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =a[2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2})\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2ax\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+2bx\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =a[{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2})\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- The second operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} \\  & =a[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}]+b[{x}^{3}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}] \\  & =a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2})\,{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is **not** linear.
To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2}) & =a[{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+x{y}_{1}]+b[{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+x{y}_{2}] \\  & =a{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ax{y}_{1}+bx{y}_{2}.\,{\color{red}\times }\end{aligned}
$$

$$
L(ay_1 + by_2) = aL(y_1) + bL(y_2)
$$

for functions $y_1(x), y_2(x),$ and where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

For the given differential operator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})(a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}})+a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =+{a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ab{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+ab{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} \\  & +a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & +ab({y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}).\end{aligned}
$$

This is *not* the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2}) & =a[{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{y}_{1}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{y}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $D(ay_1+by_2)  \neq aD(y_1) + bD(y_2),$ the operator $D$ is nonlinear.

D_3(y) = f_{3}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{3}y}{\textrm d x^{3}} + f_{2}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}} + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y
$$

with $f_3(x) = 1, f_2(x) = e^{x}, f_1(x) = 0,$ and $f_0(x) = -\ln(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

solution_sources.name: Example: Identifying Linear Differential Operators Using the General Form
solution_sources.problem:
Which of the following are linear differential operators?

I. $D_1(y)=\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x}+x\cos(y)\,y$

II. $D_2(y)=\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}}-\sin(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x}+3y$

III. $D_3(y)=\dfrac{\textrm d^{3}y}{\textrm d x^{3}}+e^{x}\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}}-\ln(x)\,y$
solution_sources.worked_solution:
An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y) = f_{n}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n}y}{\textrm d x^{n}} + f_{n-1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n-1}y}{\textrm d x^{n-1}} + \cdots + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y
$$

where each $f_i$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator $D_1$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the second term is $x\cos(y),$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

- Operator $D_2$ is linear. It is a second-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
D_2(y) = f_{2}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}} + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y
$$

with $f_2(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+x^2}, f_1(x) = -\sin(x),$ and $f_0(x) = 3.$

- Operator $D_3$ is linear. It is a third-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
D_3(y) = f_{3}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{3}y}{\textrm d x^{3}} + f_{2}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{2}y}{\textrm d x^{2}} + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y
$$

with $f_3(x) = 1, f_2(x) = e^{x}, f_1(x) = 0,$ and $f_0(x) = -\ln(x).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

For any linear differential operator,

$$
L(a{y}_{1}(x)+b{y}_{2}(x))=aL({y}_{1}(x))+bL({y}_{2}(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L({y}_{1}-2{y}_{2}) & =L({y}_{1})-2L({y}_{2}) \\  & =4x-2({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =-2{x}^{2}+4x-2 \\  & =-2({x}^{2}-2x+1) \\  & =-2(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

For any linear differential operator,

$$
L(a{y}_{1}(x)+b{y}_{2}(x))=aL({y}_{1}(x))+bL({y}_{2}(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L({y}_{1}+3{y}_{2}) & =L({y}_{1})+3L({y}_{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3\cdot x(x+1) \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3{x}^{2}+3x \\  & =({x}^{2}+3{x}^{2})+(3x-3x) \\  & =4{x}^{2}+0 \\  & =4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
L(a{y}_{1}(x)+b{y}_{2}(x))=aL({y}_{1}(x))+bL({y}_{2}(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & =2L({y}_{1})-L({y}_{2}) \\  & =2({e}^{x}+1)-(2{e}^{x}-3) \\  & =2{e}^{x}+2-2{e}^{x}+3 \\  & =(2{e}^{x}-2{e}^{x})+(2+3) \\  & =0+5 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

prompt_sources.problem:
Suppose that $L$ is a linear differential operator such that $L(y_1) = \tan^2{x}$ and $L(y_2) =2 \sec^2{x}$ for some functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x).$ What is $L(2y_1 -y_2)?$

*Hint: Use $\sec^2\theta = 1+\tan^2\theta.$*
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
For any linear differential operator $L,$ we have

$$
L(ay_1(x) + by_2(x)) = aL(y_1(x)) + bL(y_2(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & =2L({y}_{1})-L({y}_{2}) \\  & =2{\operatorname{tan} }^{2}x-2{\operatorname{sec} }^{2}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identity $1+\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x,$ we can simplify this even further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & =2{\operatorname{tan} }^{2}x-2(1+{\operatorname{tan} }^{2}x) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
L(2y_1 -y_2)=-2.
$$
